growth_story.headline: Paraguay climbed out of a lost decade on soy, beef and steadier policy; income per person is at a record high, but its growth slowed after 2015.
growth_story.arc: From 1990 to 2002 income per person went nowhere, averaging -0.1 percent a year, and it fell every year from 1998 to 2002 after a banking crisis in the second half of the 1990s wiped out about half the banks. From 2003 the record turned: growth averaged 2.6 percent a year through 2025, carried by a commodity boom that made Paraguay one of the biggest exporters of soy and beef, and by steadier economic policy. The fastest stretch was 2006 to 2015, at 3.5 percent a year, but it was never smooth, with falls in 2009 and 2012, the second after a severe drought, and big rebounds in 2010 and 2013. From 2016 to 2025 growth slowed to 1.8 percent a year, with falls in 2019, 2020 and 2022 as droughts and the pandemic hit and as productivity growth stalled after 2013. A strong 2025, at 5.4 percent, left income per person at its highest level yet.

threads.title: Weather and price swings
threads.text: Natural resources make up a large share of output and exports, so droughts and commodity price swings still move growth sharply from year to year; a drought pushed the economy into recession in 2022. Growth is steadier than it once was, but still more volatile than the region's average.

since_last_year.text: Income per person grew 5.4 percent in 2025, the fastest since 2013, and reached a new high; the World Bank says household spending and broad investment kept growth going into 2026. Since April 2026 the government has been paying off arrears to suppliers left from the pandemic years, which the World Bank expects to weigh on the fiscal deficit in the near term.

growth_story.tension: The sources describe a resilient economy that keeps beating growth forecasts, and against the regional median of 1.3 percent a year Paraguay does well. But the data show income per person growing 1.8 percent a year in 2016 to 2025, about half the 3.5 percent of the decade before, with three years of decline; the sources' headline growth figures are for total output in a growing population, not income per person.
